speaker: Michael Truell
title: Michael Truell: How Cursor Builds at the Speed of AI
question: When AI coding tools disrupt software development itself, why doesn't that dynamic immediately obsolete the companies building those tools?
guest: Two things. First, despite the headlines, despite how much demand there is in this market and how much software has changed over the last few years, it is still so far away from being automated. Building software in a professional setting—especially with anywhere from dozens to tens of thousands of people—is still inefficient, and it is really easy at an executive level to underestimate how far away we are from the limit of automating software. There is a really long, messy middle. Second, one of the key challenges facing the company is that we are in a market that has had an iPod moment and is going to have an iPhone moment and another iPhone moment. We have tried to build a company that can continually build those next shifts, because if we do not, we are kaput. At the same time, those physics are one of the nice things about the space, because they make it pretty tricky for large incumbents like Microsoft to really compete in a big way.

points.core: Large-scale professional software engineering remains far from full end-to-end automation.
points.note: Accept: explaining that real-world production software built across large organizations remains deeply inefficient and leaves a long "messy middle" that executives underestimate. Do not credit: claiming AI coding has plateaued or will never improve.

points.core: Surviving repeated AI paradigm shifts requires continually reinventing the core product.
points.note: Accept: noting that AI coding undergoes successive generational form-factor shifts (not a single one-time transition), so companies must repeatedly cannibalize or rebuild their own product to survive. Do not credit: assuming a one-time product moat guarantees survival.

points.core: Frequent paradigm shifts structurally handicap slow-moving legacy incumbents trying to compete.
points.note: Accept: explaining that rapid, recurring platform shifts act as a structural advantage for agile startups because giant incumbents struggle to reinvent their products fast enough. Do not credit: claiming incumbents automatically win due to distribution.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Because writing code was never the scarce thing these companies sell. When AI makes code cheap, value shifts to whatever remains hard, and the toolmakers tend to hold exactly those assets.

The frontier model labs own the bottleneck inputs: massive compute, research talent, proprietary training data and the capital to keep spending. Cheaper software doesn't replicate a data centre or a training run. Their tools also improve their own development first, so the disruption compounds in their favour rather than against them.

Demand also expands rather than shrinks. As software gets cheaper to produce, far more of it gets built (the Jevons effect), which increases usage of the tools doing the building.

What stays valuable is distribution, enterprise trust, security and compliance, workflow integration, and usage feedback that improves the product. Deciding what to build, verifying it works and taking accountability for it still require judgment.

The protection is uneven, though. Thin "wrapper" tools built on someone else's model are exposed, since their features are easily cloned or absorbed by model providers. The dynamic doesn't spare everyone; it concentrates advantage in whoever controls the models, compute and customer relationships.

points.why: The response identifies tasks that still require human judgment but does not explain why large-scale professional software engineering remains far from end-to-end automation.
The response describes how model providers can absorb wrapper features but does not connect survival to repeatedly reinventing the core product as successive AI paradigms emerge.
The response emphasizes control of models, compute, and customer relationships without explaining how recurring platform shifts handicap slow-moving incumbents.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
AI coding tools commoditize writing code, not the scarce inputs required to build and scale frontier developer platforms. When syntax generation becomes cheap, competitive advantage shifts from raw application code to assets a newcomer cannot simply prompt into existence. Leading toolmakers depend on massive compute, custom model post-training, rigorous evaluation harnesses, and low-latency inference infrastructure grounded in capital and specialized research rather than routine programming.

Crucially, live deployment powers a proprietary data flywheel: millions of real-world edits, rejections, and debugging traces continuously refine context retrieval and agent behavior in ways static clones cannot match. Enterprise adoption further depends on security certifications, governance, organizational trust, and entrenched workflow distribution—moats that remain immune to instant code replication. Meanwhile, the toolmakers capture their own productivity gains first, using internal systems to compound their speed of research and iteration. Finally, Jevons paradox takes hold: lowering the cost of producing code dramatically expands total software creation and system complexity, increasing demand for trusted platforms that orchestrate, verify, and maintain software at scale.

points.why: The response predicts rising demand for orchestration, verification, and maintenance but leaves unaddressed how far large-scale professional software engineering remains from end-to-end automation.
The response credits faster research and iteration without explaining why repeated AI paradigm shifts require toolmakers to reinvent their core products to survive.
The response cites entrenched distribution as a moat and leaves unaddressed why recurring paradigm shifts disadvantage incumbents that adapt slowly.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
AI coding tools make code cheaper to write, but code was never the main moat for the companies building them. Their scarce assets are frontier models, which take enormous compute, capital, research talent and proprietary training data. They also have usage feedback loops: millions of developers' accept and reject signals help improve the next model. And they have distribution, enterprise trust, security compliance and integrations, none of which a competitor can quickly rebuild just because coding got easier.

These companies are also the first and heaviest users of their own tools. They ship faster with them, so the speedup works in their favour before it works against them.

Cheaper software also tends to raise demand rather than shrink it, a Jevons-paradox effect. More people build more software, and that means more demand for the tools.

The disruption is real, though. It hits thin "wrapper" products hardest, meaning apps built on someone else's model with little of their own underneath. Switching costs are low and model providers can absorb their features. So the tool makers aren't immune. The pressure falls on whichever layer has no defensible inputs, and over time value moves toward compute, models and data.

points.why: The response discusses cheaper code and rising demand but never explains why large-scale professional software engineering remains far from end-to-end automation.
Shipping faster and defending against feature absorption do not establish that successive paradigm shifts require companies to repeatedly reinvent their core products.
The response cites distribution and enterprise trust as advantages but never connects recurring paradigm shifts to legacy incumbents’ difficulty reinventing their products quickly.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
When AI coding tools make writing code dramatically cheaper, they do not eliminate the need for software development infrastructure; they shift where the hard problems live. As raw code generation becomes commoditized, the bottleneck moves to context management, verification, security, and safely integrating changes into complex production systems. Toolmakers are uniquely positioned to capture that higher layer because they already sit inside the developer workflow, collecting feedback loops on which edits succeed or fail to continuously improve their agents.

Moreover, cheaper code tends to trigger a Jevons paradox: organizations build and maintain far more software, expanding demand for tools that govern and scale that output. Enterprises also pay for compliance, permissions, accountability, and deep integration with existing repositories and pipelines—not just raw model output. Finally, because these companies aggressively use their own tools, they can evolve quickly from simple autocomplete toward full agentic orchestration rather than being stranded by the shift they accelerated.

points.why: The response identifies production bottlenecks that persist as code generation gets cheaper but leaves open how far professional software engineering is from end-to-end automation.
The response describes one transition from autocomplete to agentic orchestration without establishing that survival requires repeated product reinvention.
The response credits toolmakers with adapting quickly but does not explain how recurring shifts put legacy incumbents at a structural disadvantage.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
AI coding tools make it cheaper to build software, including rival coding tools. The companies building them get the same productivity gains and can use them to improve their products faster. The race speeds up for everyone.

Generating code is only one part of delivering a tool people will pay for. Companies also need to make it work reliably across messy codebases, integrate it into existing workflows, and earn enough trust that customers will give it access to their code. An incumbent can draw on customer relationships, real-world feedback, and integrations that take time for competitors to replicate.

Those advantages can erode. If models become interchangeable and customers can switch easily, prices may fall and more of the profit may go to whoever controls the models or the platform developers already use. The productivity gain can arrive overnight. The shift in who captures the value takes longer.

points.why: The response describes barriers to making coding tools commercially useful, leaving unaddressed how far large-scale professional software engineering remains from end-to-end automation.
The response describes faster product improvement and possible commoditization without explaining why successive paradigm shifts require companies to repeatedly reinvent their core product.
The response highlights incumbents’ customer relationships and integrations without explaining how recurring shifts make it harder for large incumbents to keep pace.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
AI coding tools make software cheaper to build, including for the companies that make them. A rival can use AI to copy a feature faster, but the incumbent can use the same tools to improve its product faster. And copying a feature doesn’t instantly give the rival customers’ trust, a place in their workflows, or the feedback that shows which problems are worth solving.

The long-term threat is real. If competing tools become interchangeable and switching is easy, prices and margins can fall even as usage grows. But cheaper development changes the terms of competition. It doesn’t, by itself, give customers a reason to switch.

points.why: The response says AI lowers development costs but does not explain why large-scale professional software engineering remains far from end-to-end automation.
The response discusses faster product improvement without explaining why successive AI paradigm shifts require companies to repeatedly reinvent their core product.
The response describes advantages that existing vendors retain without explaining why recurring shifts make it harder for slow-moving legacy incumbents to compete.
